criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and matches Exclusion Criterion 7): the study examines watershed-scale water resource management and agricultural irrigation water extraction (over 90% of aquifer water used for crops such as chilli, pecans, cotton, alfalfa, sorghum and maize across upstream Mennonite farms and downstream Irrigation District El Carmen 089), with no analysis of household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines legal, institutional and governance factors (Mexico's National Water Law concession regime, the 1957 restricted-access presidential decree, CONAGUA inspection/enforcement gaps, corruption/apocryphal water rights, court injunctions and River Basin Councils). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, although water-rights permitting, restricted-access rules and enforcement are rule-type legal mechanisms, here they govern agricultural irrigation and raw watershed resource extraction rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (so narrow c2 = no). Because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 fail regardless, the overall full-text decision under both the plain wording and narrow reading of Criterion 2 is exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3: empirical qualitative case study based on 27 semi-structured interviews with watershed stakeholders conducted in February-April 2018, analysed using deductive content analysis in NVivo 11 and triangulated with official government secondary data.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: outcomes examined are aquifer overexploitation/depletion, reduced surface water flow, illegal irrigation dams and wells, grassland-to-cropland conversion, and violent inter-group conflict over agricultural irrigation water rather than household or community water/sanitation service access, connection, continuity or affordability.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies Criterion 5: population and sample (27 stakeholders in the Rio del Carmen watershed, Chihuahua, Mexico; unit of analysis is the watershed social-ecological governance system and agricultural water users), legal/governance exposure, ecological/conflict outcomes and qualitative case-study design are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6: full text is published in English (with Spanish interviews translated into English by the authors).

evidence_quotes.quote: More than 90% of water from these aquifers is used for agricultural purposes (CONAGUA, 2015a), producing mainly chilli, pecans, cotton, alfalfa, sorghum, and maize (Lopez Porras et al., 2018).

Article 27 of the Political Constitution of Mexico establishes that the State is the original owner of water resources located within national territory, and the use or exploitation of water can only be made through concessions granted by the federal government.
This means that new applications for water rights in the watershed will only be issued if studies determine that there is water available (LAN, 2016).
27 semi-structured interviews were conducted with key stakeholders in the watershed, in order to understand the water governance structure and its system dynamics.

On the whole, it can be observed that water governance in the Rio del Carmen watershed does not regulate water access in relation to availability as established by CONAGUA; on the contrary, water is accessed according to the number and types of crops that farmers wish to harvest

raw_response.exposure: Water governance and legal/institutional framework in the Rio del Carmen watershed (National Water Law concessions, 1957 restricted-access decree, CONAGUA administration, corruption/false water rights, judicial defence injunctions and lack of enforcement)
raw_response.outcome: Illegal agricultural water extraction, aquifer overexploitation, surface water depletion, grassland loss and violent conflicts between upstream Mennonite and downstream Mexican farmers over irrigation water
raw_response.population_and_sample: Watershed stakeholders related to agricultural water governance in the Rio del Carmen watershed, Chihuahua, Mexico (purposeful and snowball sample of n = 27 interviewees: 14 Mennonite and Mexican farmers, 7 government officials, 4 consultants, 1 NGO representative and 1 academic; unit of analysis: watershed governance system and agricultural water users)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E07 (Wrong service; Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). This qualitative empirical study investigates adaptive watershed governance, CONAGUA water-rights concessions, corruption and farmer conflicts over agricultural irrigation water and water ecosystem services in the Rio del Carmen watershed, Chihuahua, Mexico. Over 90% of aquifer extraction is for commercial/agricultural crop irrigation (pecans, maize, chilli, cotton, alfalfa, sorghum), and the paper does not examine household or community drinking-water supply or sanitation service access.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative case study using semi-structured stakeholder interviews (n = 27) with deductive content analysis and secondary data triangulation
